newsitem.title: USA: Alcoa concerned over possible manipulation.
newsitem.headline: Alcoa concerned over possible manipulation.

text.p: Paul O'Neill, chairman and CEO of Alcoa, the world's biggest aluminum producer, has expressed concern about possible market manipulation and urged better tracking of metal flows, analysts said.
O'Neill made his comments to analysts at a briefing in New York on Monday.
Clarence Morrison, analyst with Prudential Securities and present at Alcoa's briefing, said the company was now formalizing its suggestions in a memo to regulatory authorities about his concerns.
"It's the first instance in which a major aluminum producer has come out to state the need for greater regulation," Morrison said.
An Alcoa spokesperson was unable to comment immediately.

According to several analysts at the briefing, Alcoa's chairman wanted a better way to track metal flows from producers to end users, and questioned the way aluminum is put on and off warrant and how this influenced the market, analysts noted.
"He simply said much greater control was needed by the regulatory authorities of the terminal markets," said one analyst at the meeting.
O'Neill did not want to see a Sumitomo-type debacle hitting the aluminum market, the analysts added.
LME is already taking steps that should meet some of O'Neill's concerns, analysts said.
From October 1 the LME will start recording metal that has been taken off warrant but not physically shipped out of the warehouse. This willl apply to all metals on the exchange.
The change stems from a U.K financial watchdog recommendation following its post-Sumitomo probe into LME.
Some observers believe this reporting may be eventually extended to report metal that is delivered into an LME warehouse but not yet put on warrant.
Last week traders noted that 10,000 tonnes of off-warrant consignment aluminum was put on warrant in Rotterdam, but this had been widely expected.
Alcoa's concerns will, nevertheless strike a chord in the market, analysts said.
"I think a lot of CEOs are having a hard time dealing with the fundamentals which appear to be improving, and yet you have a lackluster metal price." analysts said.
